objective.statement: Choose chords that fit the marked notes at the end of a phrase and name the cadence they make.
successCriteria: For any marked melody note I can list every chord from I, ii, IV and V that contains it.
I can choose a pair of chords that makes a perfect, plagal or imperfect cadence.
I can recognise when more than one answer is correct, and explain why.

explanation.text: A cadence is the pair of chords at the end of a phrase — musical punctuation. Ending on chord I sounds finished: V–I is a perfect cadence and IV–I is a plagal cadence. Ending on chord V sounds like a comma: I–V, ii–V or IV–V make an imperfect cadence.

To harmonise a cadence point, work one note at a time. A chord fits a melody note only if that note belongs to the chord. Write down every chord (from I, ii, IV and V) that contains the note, then pick a pair that makes a cadence.
Sometimes two different chords both fit. That's fine — in music there is often more than one good answer. Any choice that contains the melody note and makes a real cadence is correct.
In this lesson every melody is in C, G, D or F major, and you can give chords as roman numerals (ii, V), as letter names (a–c–e) or by writing them on the stave.

music.textAlternative: Two bars in D major, 3/4. Bar 1: F sharp, A, D (crotchets). Bar 2: E (minim, labelled X), D (crotchet, labelled Y).

steps: Highlight note X (E). The chord grid shows which of I (D–F♯–A), ii (E–G–B), IV (G–B–D) and V (A–C♯–E) contain E: ii and V.
Highlight note Y (D). D is in I (D–F♯–A) and IV (G–B–D).
Try each pairing. V–I is a perfect cadence. ii–I, ii–IV and V–IV are not cadences, so they are crossed out.
Play V–I under the melody (optional sound) and see the finished-sounding perfect cadence.
demonstration.textAlternative: The chord grid is also presented as a table: for each marked note, the chords containing it; then the list of pairs with 'cadence' or 'not a cadence' beside each.

guided.prompt: In G major, which of these chords contain the note C? Choose all that apply.
hints: Spell each chord out and look for C.
Two of the chords contain C.

feedback.correct: Yes — C is in ii (A–C–E) and in IV (C–E–G).

mistakes.chord-lacks-melody-note: Check the notes: I is G–B–D and V is D–F♯–A, so neither contains C.
mistakes.wrong-key: Build the chords in G major: remember the F♯.

feedback.fallback: C belongs to ii (A–C–E) and IV (C–E–G).

guided.prompt: A phrase in F major ends with chord V (C–E–G) followed by chord I (F–A–C). What cadence is this?
hints: Which chord does it end on?

feedback.correct: Right — V–I is a perfect cadence.

mistakes.cadence-misnamed: It ends on I, so it can't be imperfect. Coming from V (not IV) makes it perfect.

independent.prompt: Choose a suitable chord (I, ii, IV or V) for each of the notes marked A, B, C and D. Then name the cadence formed by A–B and by C–D.

music.textAlternative: Four bars in G major, 4/4, Moderato. Bar 1: G, B, D, B (crotchets). Bar 2: C (minim, A), A (minim, B). Bar 3: B, D, C, A (crotchets). Bar 4: F sharp (minim, C), G (minim, D).

hints: List the chords that contain each marked note.
Bar 2 ends on chord V; bar 4 ends on chord I.

feedback.correct: Excellent. A can be ii or IV — both contain C and both lead to V — so A–B is an imperfect cadence. C must be V (only V contains F♯) and D is I, so C–D is a perfect cadence.

mistakes.chord-lacks-melody-note: One of your chords doesn't contain its melody note. For example, F♯ (note C) is only in chord V (D–F♯–A).
mistakes.non-cadential-pair: Your chords contain the right notes but don't make a cadence. Note B (A) could be in ii or V — but only V makes a cadence here.
mistakes.cadence-misnamed: Look at where each phrase ends: bar 2 ends on V (imperfect); bar 4 goes V–I (perfect).
mistakes.wrong-key: Remember the key is G major (F♯). Chord V is D–F♯–A.

feedback.fallback: A: ii or IV; B: V (imperfect cadence). C: V; D: I (perfect cadence).

independent.prompt: Choose a chord for each of the notes marked A and B, and name the cadence.

music.textAlternative: Two bars in F major, 4/4. Bar 1: F, A, C, A (crotchets). Bar 2: B flat (minim, A), A (minim, B).

hints: Which chords contain A? Only one of I, ii, IV, V does.
Then which chord containing B♭ can come before it as a cadence?

feedback.correct: Correct — B (A) is only in chord I, and of the chords containing B♭ (ii and IV) only IV makes a cadence with I: a plagal cadence.

mistakes.chord-lacks-melody-note: Check the chord notes: in F major, I = F–A–C, ii = G–B♭–D, IV = B♭–D–F, V = C–E–G.
mistakes.non-cadential-pair: ii–I is not one of the cadences. With B♭ in the melody, IV–I (plagal) works.
mistakes.cadence-misnamed: IV–I is a plagal cadence (not perfect, which is V–I).

feedback.fallback: A: IV; B: I — a plagal cadence.

independent.prompt: A phrase in D major ends with chord I (D–F♯–A) followed by chord V (A–C♯–E). What cadence is this?

feedback.correct: Yes — any cadence ending on V is imperfect.

mistakes.cadence-misnamed: Look at the last chord: it's V, and a cadence ending on V is imperfect.

recap: A chord fits a melody note only if the note belongs to the chord.
Perfect = V–I, plagal = IV–I, imperfect = I, ii or IV going to V.
If several chords fit and still make a cadence, every one of them is correct.

mastery.completion: Complete when all steps have been attempted. Mastery evidence comes only from first-attempt, hint-free independent steps; a hinted answer is recorded as learning, not mastery.

provenance.authoredBy: Music Theory Path curriculum team (Brief 01 example)
provenance.notes: All melodies are newly composed for this lesson. Accepted answers are re-derived by the curriculum validator from the melody notes and the cadence rules, so they cannot silently drift.
